body.heading: A spoon with a secret job
paragraphs: Long ago, engineers built giant catapults to throw heavy stones over castle walls. Yours fits on a table and throws something much friendlier: a pom-pom. But the science is exactly the same — store up energy, then let it go all at once.

body.heading: Meet the parts
paragraphs: The arm — the spoon. Its bowl is the bucket that holds your pom-pom. The base — a bottle cap or small block the spoon rests across; this is the fulcrum, the tipping point. The band — a rubber band that holds the spoon down and stretches to store energy. The load — your soft pom-pom, the only thing allowed to fly.

body.heading: You will need
paragraphs: A plastic spoon, a bottle cap or small wooden block, a rubber band, tape, a soft pom-pom or cotton ball, and a paper target to aim at. That is all — no tools at all.

paragraphs: Step 1 — Rest the spoon across the bottle cap like a tiny seesaw, bowl end up. Tape the cap to the table so the base cannot wander.
Step 2 — Loop the rubber band over the spoon's handle end and anchor it to the table or a heavy book, so the handle is held down and the bowl end points up.
Step 3 — Load the pom-pom into the bowl. Press the bowl end down gently — feel the band stretch. That stretch is stored energy, waiting.
Step 4 — Let go! The band snaps the arm back, the arm whips up, and the pom-pom flies. Try pressing down a little and then a lot. More stretch, more stored energy, longer flight.

body.heading: The science bit
paragraphs: A stretched rubber band holds potential energy — energy stored by being stretched or squashed. When you let go, that stored energy turns into movement energy in a flash. The arm swings, the bucket stops suddenly, and the pom-pom keeps going — flying things always try to keep moving in the direction they started.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. What happened when you pressed the spoon down further before letting go? Why?
2. Real catapult engineers aimed carefully. What could you change to make your pom-pom land closer to the target every time?

takeaway: A catapult stores energy in a stretched band and releases it in one snap — the arm swings, stops, and the soft load keeps flying.
materials: Bottle cap or small wooden block (fulcrum base)
Soft pom-pom or cotton ball (the only flying object)
supervision: A grown-up builds alongside the child and supervises every launch from start to finish.
safetyNotes: Only soft pom-poms or cotton balls may be launched — never stones, coins, food or anything hard, even as a joke.
Always launch in one agreed direction, toward the target, and check the flight path is clear of people and pets before every single launch.
Rubber bands can snap — a grown-up checks the band for cracks, and nobody pulls a band toward their own or anyone else's face.
screenFreeExtension: Target tournament: draw three paper targets at different distances, score 1, 3 and 5 points, and play first-to-20 with a family member — best of three launches each turn.
